name: Swahili
family: Niger-Congo, Atlantic-Congo, Bantu (Sabaki group, Guthrie G.42)
variety: Standard Swahili (Kiswahili Sanifu), based on the Unguja dialect of Zanzibar town; coastal (Mombasa) differences are noted where they matter
sources: Contini-Morava, Ellen (1997). Swahili phonology. In Alan S. Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Polomé, Edgar C. (1967). Swahili Language Handbook. Washington, DC: Center for Applied Linguistics.
Tucker, A. N. & Ashton, E. O. (1942). Swahili phonetics. African Studies 1.
Ashton, E. O. (1944). Swahili Grammar (Including Intonation). London: Longmans, Green.
Maw, Joan & Kelly, John (1975). Intonation in Swahili. London: School of Oriental and African Studies.
Engstrand, Olle & Lodhi, Abdulaziz Y. (1985). On aspiration in Swahili: hypotheses, field observations, and an instrumental analysis. Phonetica 42.
Ladefoged, Peter & Maddieson, Ian (1996). The Sounds of the World's Languages. Oxford: Blackwell.
Maddieson, Ian (2003). The sounds of the Bantu languages. In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages. London: Routledge.
Sungita, Y. Y. & Mhamilawa, E. E. (2006). Formant analysis for Kiswahili vowels. Tanzania Journal of Science 32(1).
contrasts: five vowel qualities, with no phonemic length, nasalisation or reduction
three stop series: voiceless, voiced implosive (ɓ ɗ ʄ ɠ) and prenasalised voiced (ᵐb ⁿd ⁿdʒ ᵑɡ)
velar nasal ŋ (written ng') versus prenasalised ᵑɡ (written ng)
syllabic nasals (mtu, nchi) versus non-syllabic prenasalisation (mbuzi, ndizi)
dental fricatives θ ð and velar fricatives x ɣ in words of Arabic origin
aspirated versus unaspirated voiceless stops in coastal varieties (pʰaa 'gazelle' versus paa 'roof'); not written and not kept by all standard speakers
allophony: voiced stops are implosive [ɓ ɗ ʄ ɠ] word-initially and between vowels, and plain [b d dʒ ɡ] after a homorganic nasal
/ʄ/ (written j) ranges from a palatal implosive or stop to an affricate [dʒ]; the affricate is usual after a nasal
/r/ is an alveolar tap or short trill [ɾ ~ r]
/ɛ ɔ/ are open-mid; Polomé (1967) reports closer [e o] and laxer [ɪ ʊ] for the mid and high vowels in unstressed syllables, Contini-Morava (1997) reports no reduction
the class prefixes m- before a consonant and n- before a monosyllabic stem are syllabic: mtu [ˈm̩.tu], mtoto [m̩.ˈtɔ.tɔ], nchi [ˈn̩.tʃi]
/x/ is often replaced by [h], /ɣ/ by [ɡ] and /θ ð/ by [s z] in colloquial speech
many speakers whose first language lacks the contrast interchange /l/ and /r/
syllable_structure: (N)(C)(G)V and syllabic N̩; all syllables are open (G = w or j)
phonotactics: no codas in native words; clusters in loans are usually broken by an inserted vowel
consonant plus glide onsets are common (bw, mw, kw, py, vy)
adjacent vowels are separate syllables; two identical vowels (kaa, juu, kondoo) count as two syllables for stress and sound like one long vowel
nasal plus consonant sequences are homorganic; a nasal before a voiceless stop is always syllabic

stress.rule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, counting a syllabic nasal as a syllable (mtu [ˈm̩tu]); a few Arabic loans keep antepenultimate stress in careful speech (barabara 'exactly' [baˈrabara] versus barabara 'road' [baraˈbara]).
stress.cues: higher pitch, longer vowel and greater intensity on the penultimate syllable; vowel quality stays the same

rhythm.notes: Lengthening goes to the stressed penultimate syllable, the final syllable is short. The rhythm class is the traditional description; I know of no published nPVI value.

length.notes: Length is not contrastive on a single vowel. Double vowel letters (from loss of l between vowels and from Arabic loans) are treated as two syllables, of which the first is stressed when they end the word; phonetically the result is a long vowel. The stressed penultimate vowel is longer than the others.

intonation.declarative: pitch peak on each stressed penultimate syllable with gradual downdrift; the last stressed syllable falls to a low final syllable
intonation.yes_no_question: same word order as a statement, optionally with initial je; raised register with less downdrift, the last stressed syllable is high and the fall comes late on the final syllable
intonation.wh_question: the question word (nani, nini, wapi, lini) stays in place, often at the end of the clause, and takes the main high-falling accent
intonation.continuation: non-final phrases end on a sustained or rising pitch
intonation.accent_shape: high or rising pitch on the penultimate syllable, falling on the final syllable
intonation.notes: After Ashton (1944) and Maw & Kelly (1975). These are auditory descriptions; instrumental work on Swahili intonation is scarce.

tone.notes: Standard Swahili has lost the lexical and grammatical tone found in most Bantu languages; pitch serves stress and intonation only.

phonation: implosive (glottalic ingressive) voiced stops ɓ ɗ ʄ ɠ
aspiration of voiceless stops in coastal varieties

problems: the velar nasal written ng' fails at the start of a word: ng'ombe and ng'ambo are read as the letter names of n and g followed by the rest of the word, whether the apostrophe is ASCII, U+2019 or U+02BC; inside a word (kung'aa) it is [ŋ], but the word is followed by an unwanted pause
b, d, j, g are plain pulmonic voiced stops everywhere; there are no implosive phonemes, so the implosive versus post-nasal plain alternation is missing
word-initial m or n before a consonant is syllabic only when it has to carry the penultimate stress (mtu, mbwa, nchi); in longer words (mtoto, mchezo, mkate) it is a plain non-syllabic nasal
kh is pronounced as k followed by h, not as the velar fricative [x]; the rule for [x] is shadowed by a rule for k
prenasalised stops are full nasal plus stop sequences, with no control of the short nasal portion
no aspirated stops for coastal varieties
good: penultimate stress, including on syllabic nasals
five vowels without reduction; adjacent vowels kept as separate syllables
dh, th, gh, sh, ch, ny digraphs are mapped to ð, θ, ɣ, ʃ, tʃ, ɲ

notes: No vowel formant block is given. The one published table I could check (Sungita & Mhamilawa 2006: one male speaker, vowels read off spectrograms of digit words, signal limited to 4 kHz) gives roughly i 370/2060, e 530/1735, a 775/1355, o 560/950 and u 530/920 Hz for F1/F2, but its F1 for /u/ (500 to 562 Hz) is implausibly high, so the values are not reliable enough to drive a synthesiser.
